h.strategy: Use retrieved findings to classify settings as strong, weak, neutral or harmful, and to identify which settings can disconnect other parts from the outcome. Propose hypotheses only of two kinds. Self-conditioning: the edit's effect depends on the value it replaces, being more negative when that value is strong and more positive when it is empty or harmful. Disconnection: when the edited part cannot influence the outcome, its effect shrinks toward zero, so the direction is lower if the edit usually helps and higher if it usually hurts. Directions refer to the signed effect. For each hypothesis, state the edit's usual sign and a one-sentence mechanism. Cover varied edit fields and values. The critic should replace any hypothesis with an uncertain usual sign, competing effects or reliance on partial redundancy.

hyps.why: Replacing a weak pool on the final deep-path edge with a strong conv gains more than replacing skip, conv1x1 or none.
Deleting a strong conv on edge 0 removes the most capacity from both paths through node 1.
Filling an empty input-output edge adds a path, whereas replacing a skip there discards a useful residual.
Replacing a harmful pool feeding node 2 with a conv gains more than replacing a conv or skip.
With edge 0 none, node 1 is zero, so a conv on edge 4 has no input and its usual gain vanishes.
With edge 5 none, node 2 cannot reach the output, so a conv on edge 2 cannot help.
With node 2 disconnected from the output, the usual harm of a pool on edge 1 shrinks toward zero.
Node 1 is zero when edge 0 is none, so a conv applied to it on edge 2 adds nothing.
With edge 5 none, the pooled output on edge 2 never reaches node 3, so its harm disappears.
With edge 5 absent, edge 3 is one of only two inputs to the output node, so deleting it is far more damaging.
